# Section A — The relatives of a statement

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise K, Q2–3</span>

::: {.question}
Let $S$ be the statement "if $A$ then $B$".

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** What is the contrapositive of the converse of $S$? Is it logically equivalent to $S$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** What is the converse of the contrapositive of $S$? Is it logically equivalent to $S$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**Both are the inverse of $S$, and neither is equivalent to $S$.**

**(a)** The converse of $S$ is $B\Rightarrow A$. Its contrapositive negates and swaps:

$$\text{not }A\Rightarrow\text{not }B .$$

**(b)** The contrapositive of $S$ is $\text{not }B\Rightarrow\text{not }A$. Its converse swaps:

$$\text{not }A\Rightarrow\text{not }B .$$

Both routes give the **inverse**. It is equivalent to the converse, and it is broken by the row "$A$ false, $B$
true", whereas $S$ is broken by "$A$ true, $B$ false". Different breaking rows mean different statements.
:::

## Question 2 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
The first seven terms of a sequence of positive integers are:

$$u_1=15,\quad u_2=21,\quad u_3=30,\quad u_4=37,\quad u_5=44,\quad u_6=51,\quad u_7=59$$

Consider the following statement about this sequence:

> $(*)$ If $n$ is a prime number, then $u_n$ is a multiple of $3$ or $u_n$ is a multiple of $5$.

What is the smallest value of $n$ that provides a counterexample to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $6$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $7$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E — $n=5$.**

A counterexample needs the hypothesis **true** and the conclusion **false**. Negating the "or", the conclusion
is false when $u_n$ is a multiple of neither $3$ nor $5$.

| $n$ | $n$ prime? | $u_n$ | multiple of $3$ or $5$? | counterexample? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | no | $15$ | — | no |
| $2$ | yes | $21$ | yes | no |
| $3$ | yes | $30$ | yes | no |
| $4$ | no | $37$ | — | no |
| $5$ | yes | $44$ | **no** | **yes** |

$n=4$ is the trap: $37$ fails the conclusion, but $4$ is not prime, so the statement says nothing about it.
:::

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Let $n$ denote a positive integer. Consider the following three statements.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** For every $n$, if $n^2$ is divisible by $12$, then $n$ is divisible by $6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** For every $n$, if $n^2$ is divisible by $12$, then $n$ is divisible by $12$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** There exists an $n$ such that $n^2$ is divisible by $12$ but $n$ is not divisible by $12$.

Which of the statements are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** all of them
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**F — I and III only.**

**I is true.** Use the contrapositive idea on primes. $n^2$ divisible by $3$ forces $3\mid n$, since $3$ is
prime. $n^2$ divisible by $4$ forces $n$ even, since an odd $n$ has an odd square. So $2\mid n$ and $3\mid n$,
which gives $6\mid n$.

**II is false.** Take $n=6$. Then $n^2=36=12\times3$, but $12$ does not divide $6$.

**III is true.** The same $n=6$ works. **III is exactly the negation of II**: a "hypothesis true, conclusion
false" case. So one of II and III had to be true and the other false.
:::

## Question 4 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the statement about Fred:

> $(*)$ Every day next week, Fred will do at least one maths problem.

If statement $(*)$ is **not** true, which of the following is certainly true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Every day next week, Fred will do more than one maths problem.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Some day next week, Fred will do more than one maths problem.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** On no day next week will Fred do more than one maths problem.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Every day next week, Fred will do no maths problems.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** Some day next week, Fred will do no maths problems.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** On no day next week will Fred do no maths problems.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E.**

To use a contrapositive you must be able to negate. "$(*)$ is not true" means there is at least one day that
breaks it, and nothing more.

- Negating "every day" gives "some day".
- Negating "at least one problem" gives "no problems".

So the negation is "some day next week, Fred will do no maths problems".

**D is the tempting wrong answer.** It over-negates: one failing day is enough, and $(*)$ can be false while
Fred works on the other six days. Session 4 covers this in full.
:::

# Section B — What follows, and what does not

## Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
$a,b$ and $c$ are real numbers.

Given that $ab=ac$, which of the following statements must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $a=0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** $b=0$ or $c=0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** $b=c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A — none of them.**

Do not divide by $a$, since $a$ might be zero. Rearrange and factorise instead:

$$ab-ac=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(b-c)=0 .$$

So what follows is the **"or"**: $a=0$ or $b=c$. Neither half follows on its own.

- **I fails:** $a=1,\ b=c=2$ satisfies $ab=ac$, and $a\ne0$.
- **II fails:** the same example has $b$ and $c$ both non-zero.
- **III fails:** $a=0,\ b=1,\ c=2$ satisfies $ab=ac$, and $b\ne c$.

Note that $b=c\Rightarrow ab=ac$ is always true. It is the **converse** that fails, which is the whole trap.
:::

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q2</span>

::: {.question}
Let $x,y,z$ be real numbers with $x\ge y$. Which of the following statements must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1** $x^3\ge y^3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**2** $x^2\ge y^2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** $xz\ge yz$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**4** $xz^2\ge yz^2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** 1 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** 4 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** 1 and 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** 1 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** 1 and 4 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** 2 and 4 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** 1, 2 and 4 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** 1, 3 and 4 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**J** 1, 2, 3 and 4
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**F — 1 and 4 only.**

Each line claims "$x\ge y\Rightarrow\dots$", so each false one needs a single counterexample.

- **1 is true.** $t^3$ is increasing on all real numbers.
- **2 is false.** $x=1,\ y=-2$ gives $1\ge4$, which fails. Squaring is not increasing on negative numbers.
- **3 is false.** $x=1,\ y=0,\ z=-1$ gives $-1\ge0$, which fails.
- **4 is true.** $z^2\ge0$, and multiplying by a non-negative number keeps the direction.
:::

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set A · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
The real numbers $a,b,c$ and $d$ satisfy $0<a<b<c<d$.

Which of the following inequalities must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $a+c<b+d$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** $d-c>b-a$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** $\dfrac bc<\dfrac da$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**G — I and III only.**

**I is true.** Add $a<b$ and $c<d$.

**II is false.** The gaps can be any sizes. Take $a=1,\ b=8,\ c=9,\ d=10$. Then $d-c=1$ and $b-a=7$.

**III is true.** Since $b<c$, we have $\dfrac bc<1$. Since $d>a>0$, we have $\dfrac da>1$. So
$\dfrac bc<1<\dfrac da$.
:::

---

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
$a,b$ and $c$ are real numbers with $a<b<c<0$.

Which of the following statements must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $ac<ab<a^2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** $b(c+a)>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** $\dfrac cb>\dfrac ab$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E — I and II only.**

All three numbers are negative, so multiplying or dividing by any of them reverses an inequality.

**I is true.** Start with $a<b<c$ and multiply through by $a<0$. This reverses both signs:

$$a^2>ab>ac,\qquad\text{which is}\qquad ac<ab<a^2 .$$

**II is true.** $c+a<0$ and $b<0$, and the product of two negatives is positive.

**III is false.** Start with $c>a$ and divide by $b<0$, which reverses the sign: $\dfrac cb<\dfrac ab$. This is
the opposite of III, so III is false for every allowed choice.
:::

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
The real numbers $a,b,c$ and $d$ satisfy both

$$0<a+b<c+d\qquad\text{and}\qquad0<a+c<b+d$$

Which of the following inequalities must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $a<d$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** $b<c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** $a+b+c+d>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**F — I and III only.**

**I is true.** Add the two right-hand inequalities:

$$a+b+a+c<c+d+b+d\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2a<2d\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a<d .$$

**II is false.** The hypotheses are symmetric in $b$ and $c$: swapping them turns each one into the other. So
if they forced $b<c$, they would also force $c<b$. For an explicit case, take $a=1,\ b=2,\ c=1,\ d=100$. Then
$0<3<101$ and $0<2<102$, but $b>c$.

**III is true.** $a+b>0$ and $c+d>a+b>0$. Adding gives $a+b+c+d>0$.
:::

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q16</span>

::: {.question}
In this question, $x_1,x_2,x_3,\dots$ is an arithmetic progression, all of whose terms are integers.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. **If** the median of the first $n$ terms of the sequence is an integer, which of the following three statements must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** The median of the first $n+2$ terms is an integer.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** The median of the first $2n$ terms is an integer.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** The median of $x_2,x_4,x_6,\dots,x_{2n}$ is an integer.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**F — I and III only.**

Let the common difference be $d$. The median of the first $k$ terms of an arithmetic progression is the mean of
the first and last terms:

$$\text{median of first }k\text{ terms}=x_1+\frac{(k-1)d}{2}.$$

The hypothesis says that $x_1+\dfrac{(n-1)d}{2}$ is an integer.

**I is true.** The median of the first $n+2$ terms is $x_1+\dfrac{(n+1)d}{2}$. This is the hypothesis value plus
$d$, so it is an integer.

**II is false.** Take $x_k=k$ and $n=3$. The median of $1,2,3$ is $2$, an integer. The median of the first six
terms is $3.5$.

**III is true.** The terms $x_2,x_4,\dots,x_{2n}$ form an arithmetic progression, and its median is the mean of
its first and last terms:

$$\frac{x_2+x_{2n}}{2}=\frac{2x_1+2nd}{2}=x_1+nd ,$$

which is always an integer, whatever the hypothesis says.
:::

# Section C — Proving the right direction

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to solve the following problem, where $a$ and $b$ are non-zero real numbers:

> Show that if $a^2-4b^3\ge0$ then there exist real numbers $x$ and $y$ such that $a=xy(x+y)$ and $b=xy$.

Consider the following attempt:

&nbsp;&nbsp;$(x-y)^2\ge0$ &nbsp; **(I)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $x^2+y^2-2xy\ge0$ &nbsp; **(II)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $(x+y)^2-4xy\ge0$ &nbsp; **(III)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $x^2y^2(x+y)^2-4x^3y^3\ge0$ &nbsp; **(IV)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $a^2-4b^3\ge0$ &nbsp; **(V)**

Which of the following best describes this attempt?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** It is incorrect, but it would be correct if written in the reverse order.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** It is incorrect, but the student has correctly proved the converse.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** It is incorrect because there is an error in line (II).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** It is incorrect because there is an error in line (III).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** It is incorrect because there is an error in line (IV).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

Use the two-line audit from the Notes.

**Check the algebra first.** Line (II) expands (I). Line (III) rewrites (II), because
$(x+y)^2-4xy=x^2+y^2-2xy$. Line (IV) multiplies (III) by $x^2y^2\ge0$, which keeps the direction.

**Now look at line (V).** Getting there uses $a=xy(x+y)$ and $b=xy$. So the student has **assumed** that such
$x,y$ exist and **concluded** that $a^2-4b^3\ge0$.

| | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Required** | $a^2-4b^3\ge0\Rightarrow$ such $x,y$ exist |
| **Proved** | such $x,y$ exist $\Rightarrow a^2-4b^3\ge0$ |

That is the converse, and each line of it is valid.

**Why not B?** Reversing the order would need steps such as (V) to (IV), which require already having $x$ and
$y$. Their existence is exactly what has to be shown.
:::

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
A student answered the following question:

> $a$ and $b$ are non-zero real numbers.
>
> Prove that the equation $x^3+ax^2+b=0$ has three distinct real roots if $27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}\right)<0$

Here is the student's solution:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** We differentiate $y=x^3+ax^2+b$ to get $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+2ax=x(3x+2a)$. Solving $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ shows that the stationary points are at $(0,b)$ and $\left(-\dfrac{2a}{3},\ b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}\right)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** If $27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}\right)<0$, then $b$ and $b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}$ must have opposite signs, and so one of the stationary points is above the $x$-axis and one is below.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** If the cubic has three distinct real roots, then one of the stationary points is above the $x$-axis and one is below.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** Hence if $27b\left(b+\dfrac{4a^3}{27}\right)<0$, then the equation has three distinct real roots.

Which one of the following options best describes the student's solution?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is a completely correct solution.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The student has instead proved the converse of the statement in the question.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The solution is wrong, because the student should have stated step II after step III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The solution is wrong, because the student should have shown the converse of the result in step II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The solution is wrong, because the student should have shown the converse of the result in step III.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E.**

Write the arrows for each step. Let $C$ be the condition, $S$ be "the stationary points are on opposite sides of
the $x$-axis", and $R$ be "three distinct real roots".

| Step | Arrow | Useful? |
|---|---|---|
| **II** | $C\Rightarrow S$ | Yes |
| **III** | $R\Rightarrow S$ | No: it points into $S$ |
| **IV** | claims $C\Rightarrow R$ | needs $C\Rightarrow S\Rightarrow R$ |

To reach $R$ from $S$, the student needed $S\Rightarrow R$, which is the **converse of step III**. Step III as
written gives a chain that does not connect.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-1.6,3.4,300); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0,3.2))
ax.plot(x,x**3-3*x**2+2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='$y=x^3-3x^2+2$')
ax.plot([0,2],[2,-2],'o',color='#d62728',label='stationary points')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.axvline(0,color='0.3',lw=1); ax.set_ylim(-5,4)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The graph shows why $S\Rightarrow R$ is in fact true, and so the theorem is fine. Only the logic of the written
solution is faulty.

**Why not B?** The student's first and last lines do target the correct statement. **Why not D?** Step II already
points the right way, from $C$ to $S$.
:::
